spans.note: Restates the research question: whether referees show bias by skin tone, moderated by implicit/explicit bias

spans.assertion: a cross-classified multilevel analysis found dark-skin-toned players were 1.40 times (95% CI [1.15,1.71]) more likely to receive a red card than light-skin-toned players
the skin-tone/red-card association was not moderated by referee countries' explicit or implicit racial bias
darker-skin-toned soccer players were more likely to receive red cards from referees
this association was not moderated by implicit or explicit racial bias
an age variable was computed by subtracting the birth year (last four characters of the birthday field) from 2013
a skin-tone rating variable was created by averaging the two raters' skin-tone scores (rater1 and rater2, coded 0-1)
Wikipedia was consulted to determine playing position for players with missing ("NA") position data
the position variable was recoded into 4 merged categories (goalkeeper, defender, midfielder, forward/winger) because Wikipedia did not provide specific enough information for certain players
merging positions into 4 categories caused some information to be lost
the merging procedure increased the number of observations with known position from 115,457 to 124,468
several predictors/covariates (skin-tone rating, height, weight, games, victories, defeats, goals, age) were grand-mean centered to improve interpretability of the intercept and interaction terms
implicit racial bias and explicit racial bias scores were standardized
players with missing skin-tone rating data (rater1/rater2) were excluded because skin tone is the main predictor

spans.note: Restates the two research questions: skin tone vs. red cards, and moderation by implicit/explicit bias

spans.assertion: a four-level multilevel negative-binomial model was used with player-referee dyads as level 1, players as level 2, clubs as level 3, and leagues as level 4, to account for interdependence in red-card likelihood across players, clubs, and leagues

spans.note: Illustrative hypothetical example (Arsenal vs. Manchester United) explaining what the multilevel structure captures

spans.assertion: a negative-binomial model was chosen because the dependent variable (number of red cards, "redCards") is a count variable

number of red cards was entered as the DV; skin-tone rating, implicit bias, explicit bias, the two skin-tone interactions, games, victories, defeats, height, weight, age, goals, and dummy-coded position were entered as predictors in the initial model

research question 1 was evaluated via the statistical significance of the skin-tone coefficient, and research question 2 via the significance of the skin-tone×implicit and skin-tone×explicit interaction coefficients
number of games was controlled for because more referee encounters increase the cumulative likelihood of a red card
victories, defeats, and number of goals were controlled for, reasoning players may foul less after a win and more aggressively after a loss
height and weight were controlled for, reasoning bigger players may have more bodily contact and thus more fouls
position was controlled for, reasoning defensive players (goalkeepers, defenders) may commit more fouls
age was controlled for, reasoning that impulsivity (linked to red cards) decreases with age, citing Steinberg et al. (2008)
in the initial model, skin-tone rating significantly predicted red cards; each 1-unit increase in skin-tone raised red-card count by 1.35x (b=0.30, SE=0.105, p=0.005)
the skin-tone×implicit-bias interaction was not statistically significant in the initial model (b=-0.14, SE=0.136, p=0.29)
the skin-tone×explicit-bias interaction was not statistically significant in the initial model (b=0.19, SE=0.140, p=0.17)
implicit and explicit racial biases did not significantly moderate the skin-tone/red-card association in the initial model

spans.note: Feedback from other researchers prompted addressing several issues with the initial approach

spans.assertion: club and league levels were dropped from the final model because club/league country was not coded as time-varying despite changing across a player's career

a cross-classified multilevel model was used in the final approach to account for non-independence among referees and referee countries (in addition to players), since referees differ in strictness and referee countries differ in red-card rates
number of games was entered as an offset variable (log of games) because a red card from 1 encounter differs from a red card from 15 encounters, changing the DV to red cards per game
covariates not statistically significant in the initial approach (height, weight, age, goals) were dropped from the final model
number of defeats and victories were dropped because they were highly correlated with number of games
the final model was a cross-classified multilevel negative-binomial model with random intercepts for players, referees, and referee countries

a cross-classified (rather than purely nested) multilevel model was needed because, although player-referee dyads were nested within referees within referee countries, players themselves were not nested within referees

in the final model, red cards was the DV; skin-tone rating, implicit bias, explicit bias, the two skin-tone interactions, and dummy-coded position were predictors, with log(games) entered as an offset variable
in the final model, skin-tone rating significantly predicted red-card risk; each 1-unit increase raised risk by 1.40x (b=0.34, SE=0.101, p<0.001)
the skin-tone×implicit-bias interaction was not significant in the final model (b=-0.11, SE=0.173, p=0.54)
the skin-tone×explicit-bias interaction was not significant in the final model (b=0.15, SE=0.167, p=0.36)
implicit and explicit racial biases did not significantly moderate the skin-tone/red-card association in the final model
